The hospital said Raphael was brought to its Accident and Emergency (A&E) Unit following a reported sudden collapse on a football pitch but arrived in a clinically unresponsive state. In a statement issued in Jos by its Public Relations Officer, Rinret Meshak, the management said it was responding to misleading reports circulating about the medical management of the deceased. It said it was presenting the verified clinical timeline of events as documented by medical personnel on duty. According to the statement, Raphael arrived at the A&E Unit at 6:05pm, accompanied by a large group of student nurses. “At immediate assessment, the patient was clinically unresponsive, pale, cold to the touch, with fixed and dilated pupils, and a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 3/15, indicating no signs of life upon arrival. “The doctor on call was immediately notified, while the nurses on duty commenced resuscitation protocols. Although the accompanying students attempted to perform intravenous cannulation themselves, the hospital’s nursing team maintained clinical protocol and established the IV line. A Random Blood Sugar (RBS) test was conducted, which read 8.4 mmol/L,” the statement said. The hospital explained that the doctor on call confirmed clinical unresponsiveness secondary to cardiac arrest, while cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) continued. It added that normal saline infusion and 200mg of intravenous Hydrocortisone were administered. According to the management, vital signs recorded on the cardiac monitor showed a body temperature of 31°C, with unrecordable pulse, blood pressure and oxygen saturation (SpO₂). It said intravenous Adrenaline was administered and supplemental oxygen provided, but the patient remained unresponsive. However, the hospital alleged that resuscitation efforts were disrupted when a large crowd of student nurses overwhelmed the A&E Unit, internal security personnel and Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) operatives on duty. “Despite repeated appeals, the agitated crowd obstructed hospital specialists from taking full control of the patient’s management, insisting on performing endotracheal intubation themselves and administering unapproved doses of IV Adrenaline (up to six ampoules) and Atropine, against the explicit medical advice of the attending physician,” the statement alleged. The management said that following prolonged resuscitation efforts, the students requested an ambulance to transfer Raphael to JUTH. It said his vital signs at the time showed a temperature of 30°C, oxygen saturation of 42 per cent, and unrecordable pulse and blood pressure. The hospital added that a second doctor on call managed to navigate through the crowd to reassess the patient and explain his critical condition to the students before granting formal consent for the transfer. It said the hospital ambulance was deployed at 8:59pm and departed at 9:05pm, accompanied by the nurse on duty, a hospital porter and student representatives. According to the statement, resuscitation continued throughout the journey, with the patient still recording a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3/15 and oxygen saturation of 42 per cent, before he was handed over to the A&E team at JUTH at 9:20pm. Defending its emergency response, NOH management said all life-saving medications, including intravenous fluids and emergency tray drugs, were deployed immediately in accordance with national emergency healthcare directives. The hospital also disclosed that during the period of disruption, another student from the same group was brought into the A&E Unit in critical condition. It said its medical team promptly attended to her and successfully stabilised her until she regained consciousness. While acknowledging the emotional distress caused by the sudden collapse and death of a colleague, the management warned that obstructing medical specialists and forcefully administering restricted emergency drugs could compromise standard clinical care. “The National Orthopaedic Hospital, Jos, remains unwavering in its commitment to saving lives, upholding medical ethics, and serving the public with professionalism. “We urge the public to disregard unverified narratives and allow peace and due process to prevail,” the statement added.
